newsitem.title: portugal: GERMANS, CZECHS CONFIDENT OF END TO OLD DISPUTE.
newsitem.headline: GERMANS, CZECHS CONFIDENT OF END TO OLD DISPUTE.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaaus said on Tuesday they believed a lingering dispute between the two states, with its roots in World War Two, could finally be resolved soon.
After talks during a European security summit in Lisbon both men said talks were coming to a successful conclusion.
"We are both convinced that the negotiations can be completed by the end of the year," said Kohl.
"Talks are practically finished...practically finished means that (really) it's finished," Klaus told a news conference.
Klaus said the deal would be initialled by foreign ministers before being ratified by the Czech and German parliaments and finally signed by himself and Kohl.
Asked when the signing would be, Klaus said: "I believe very soon." Kohl told reporters Klaus had invited him to visit Prague early next year.

The dispute concerns ethnic Germans who were expelled from Czech territory after World War Two. Nazi Germany took over the country before the outbreak of war in Europe and kept it under brutal occupation almost until the end of the war.

The so-called Sudeten Germans are the main obstacle to a parliamentary declaration of reconciliation intended to put the Czech Republic on the same friendly footing with Germany as the other countries which suffered Nazi invasion.

Kohl said in September that he wanted a text to be approved by the end of the year. Negotiations between the two governments on the declaration, which would regulate property and compensation issues, have continued in the meantime.

The Sudeten Germans, backed by the Bavarian CSU who are partners in Kohl's centre-right coalition government, have demanded Prague consult them directly and acknowledge that the expulsion of 2.5 million ethnic Germans was an injustice.

Prague has argued that the expulsion was legitimate in principle, although often carried out with regrettable brutality. It wants compensation from Germany for victims of the Nazi occupation like that already accorded to other countries.
Criticism has mounted in Germany over failure to agree the text after more than a year of tortuous negotiations.
Germany, a country which has often felt surrounded by enemies, is eager to build lasting security by bringing its Central and Eastern European neighbours into NATO and the European Union.
Following German unification in 1990, Bonn has resolved outstanding issues left over from World War Two with its neighbours -- except the problem of the Sudeten Germans.
